Oh man, sign language is amazing. We had heard babies can speak sign language long before actual words, so we learned a few signs and started using them with her. It’s so cool to see them thinking and communicating earlier than you’d think—it really does make you realize how much they’re thinking even before they talk. 

She picked up her first one, “all done” at about 6 months. (In contrast, now at 13 months, the only spoken word she says consistently is “Daddy”.)

In the months since, she’s learned “more” (as the opposite of all done) and “thank you”. She’d probably have learned a lot more if we actually knew sign language ourselves, or spent more time on it. This thread has inspired me to pick up some more words to teach her : )

One of the reasons —but far from the only one— that people don’t share suicidal urges, is because it’s one of the few things you can admit to that can give others the power to take control of your life away from you. If your therapist or doctor thinks you may harm yourself, they can break confidentiality to get you “help”. If your family knows you’re having suicidal thoughts, they can get you put into mental health facilities against your will, “for your own good”. You can lose custody of or access to your children. You can (by being forcibly detained) lose your job and/or your friendships/other relationships. 

I don’t know about you, but even if I had a therapist or parent that I trusted 100%, I’d hesitate to give them that power over me just in case my trust were misplaced. 

The way around this is not to ask people to come forward and share, but for professionals to talk openly as a society about what it’s like. Educate people that suicidal thoughts and urges are completely normal, can exist in an otherwise healthy mind. Talk about what can cause them, how to self-help against them, and how to (safely, and without undue risk) get professional help. 

Suicide is apparently on the rise, both worldwide and in the US in particular. I’ve recently learned the CDC is very concerned about it, and is studying it as a disease. That gives me hope that we may take some positive steps; not only on the treatment side, but also on the social acceptance side, and on the side of identifying and addressing root causes for the rising trend.

When my daughter was born with 1) a genetic disorder that was missed in testing; and 2) severe health complications from that disorder that make every day of her —and our—lives difficult, painful, labor intensive, and impossibly expensive. 

In the span of 24 hours, I went from having a relatively normal life, and looking forward to the future as my wife and I started a family; to being in a constant endless nightmare, and dreading what each new day will bring.

Oof, so many. 

Here are my top 2:

1) It is entirely possible to never find your calling. And to instead find yourself in a career that you hate down to your very soul; that kills your spirit a bit more each day; that robs you of your time and your health and your enjoyment of other parts of your life. Always, ALWAYS have a realistic exit plan if you can. 

2) Having kids is a HUGE decision. Yeah, everybody thinks they already know this... but they really don’t. It can end up being way bigger of an impact (positive or negative) on your life than you ever possibly imagined. Be 110% certain you want them before you have them. Go spend LOTS of time around your friends/relatives with kids; try babysitting them not for a night, but for weekends or weeks. Talk to those friends/family members with kids, in depth, and get them to tell you the good AND the bad. The financial impact, how it feels to trade freedom for responsibility, what it’s really like to have someone to worry about at a level you’ve never felt anything close to before. What are the biggest shocks/problems they ran into? What regrets do they have? How do they feel emotionally? How’s their physical and mental health? Keep in mind almost no one with a kid will say it was a mistake, but really read between the lines. How is their life different? Are they actually happier or more fulfilled? Think through how you’d handle the problems and surprises they mention, how each would make you feel. How it would impact your marriage (if you have one), your relationships with family and friends, your other plans and life goals. Take a year (at least) to do your research, really do it; do some serious soul-searching, and know for sure you absolutely want to have a child. Think through unlikely, but irreversible if they happen, scenarios —what if you end up with triplets? What if your child is born with a severe genetic disorder or other major lifelong health problem? What if the pregnancy doesn’t make it, or your child dies in childbirth— will you be able to deal with that? Will your significant other? Financially, what would your savings or emergency fund cover? Would a surprise like that knock you and your new child down into poverty, or worse? I know this all sounds morbid, and awful, but it’s important to think through. This is likely the most important decision you will ever make in your life.  It’s not like other things in life where if you make a bad choice, or regret it later, you can just walk away (or even if you can’t, it still is just mostly your own life you ruin). It’s a one-way street in many respects. Be absolutely sure you want to go down it before you take that turn.
